deep.reconstruction:
The page has three unrelated pieces.

(A) Lines 1-7: end of the argument begun on the previous page. The claim there is that there exist quartic surfaces f_4(x1..x4)=0 in P^3 on which every curve is a complete intersection of f_4 with another surface. Suppose not. Then for a curve on the surface (cut out by some F together with f) one gets an identity of the form A(x)F(x) = phi*psi*... + B(x)f(x). Here phi, psi, chi depend only on x1..x3, so they are cones projecting the curve.

This page continues as follows.
- If F=0 and f=0, one of the irreducible factors phi, psi, chi must vanish.
- Hence, after multiplying by linear forms l, m, ..., one gets l*m*...*F = A*phi + B*f.
- Hilbert then states that the plane section {l=0, f=0} is 'stets [ir]reducibel'. His reason: otherwise f would have to have the form f = g2*h2 - l*h3 (section splits into two conics) or f = g1*h3 - l*k3 (section splits into a line and a cubic), with subscripts denoting degrees. A general quartic is not of either form.
- From this he concludes phi = alpha*l + beta*f, 'etc.' My gloss: the projecting cone would itself be cut out by a plane modulo f, so the curve is a complete intersection.

The argument is only a sketch. The reduction to plane sections is not justified on the page.

(B) The ellipse problem ('Aufgabe'). Pass an ellipse of prescribed shape through 3 given points. The shape is fixed by the given minor and major axes, so only position and orientation (3 parameters) are free. The problem is stated, not solved.

(C) Main item, a precursor of Hilbert's 1892 irreducibility paper.

Setting:
- y is an algebraic function of x with f(y,x)=0, where f has integer coefficients.
- Assume y is rational for all rational x with alpha <= x <= beta, where alpha = p/q and beta = r/s are rational.
- Write f = phi_0 y^n + phi_1 y^(n-1) + ... + phi_n, with phi_i in Z[x]. Assume they do not vanish at the endpoint x = p/q.

Step 1, Möbius substitution: x = (p t + r)/(q t + s).
- t=0 gives x = r/s = beta; t -> infinity gives x -> p/q = alpha.
- So t in [0, inf) traverses the interval, rational t corresponds to rational x, and f(y,x) becomes g(y,t), polynomial in t after clearing denominators.

Step 2, binomial case: g(y,t) = psi(t) y^n - phi(t).
- Normalise (my reading of 'psi^n y = z'): put z = psi*y.
- Then z^n = psi^(n-1)*phi = chi(t), a polynomial with integer coefficients.
- Its degree is n*m (at most), where m is the degree bound of psi and phi.

Step 3 (completed on the next page):
- Substitute t = 1/4 (and further values) and rescale: (z/4^m)^n = a_0 + a_1/4 + ... + a_{mn}/4^{mn}.
- Expand z/4^m as a power series whose leading term is a root of a_0.
- Rationality of z for infinitely many rational t forces the series, i.e. z, to be a rational function of t.
- Hence y is rational in x (Satz I). The analogue for all positive integers x is Satz II.
- The general, non-binomial case is begun on the next page.
errors: The quartic-surface argument is a heuristic sketch. It does not justify why the cones phi, psi, chi reduce to plane sections, nor why phi = alpha*l + beta*f follows. The statement (Noether's theorem) was only rigorously proved later (Lefschetz).
On the page the word reads 'reducibel', but the logic ('weil sonst ...') requires 'irreducibel': the plane sections of a general quartic are irreducible. Either a slip or a misreading.
'Jeder f' must be read as 'a general f'. Special quartics, e.g. those containing lines or conics, do have reducible plane sections.
g(y,t) = psi*y^n - phi(t) is only the special binomial case, not a general identity. The general case is deferred to the next page.
z^n = chi(t) has degree at most n*m (possibly less), not necessarily exactly n*m.
The hypothesis that the phi_i do not vanish at x = p/q is needed so that no root becomes infinite at the endpoint t -> infinity. It is stated loosely.

results.what: A general quartic surface in P^3 contains only curves that are complete intersections with other surfaces (sketched proof attempt via plane sections)
results.modern_name: Noether(-Lefschetz) theorem: Picard group of a very general surface of degree >= 4 is generated by the hyperplane class

results.what: Ellipse of given axes through 3 given points (problem statement only)

An algebraic function rational at all rational points of an interval (or at all positive integers) is a rational function with rational coefficients. Proof via a Möbius map of the interval to [0, inf), reduction to the binomial case z^n = chi(t), and series expansion at t -> infinity.
results.modern_name: Corollary of Hilbert's irreducibility theorem / Hilbertian property of Q

deep.surprise_reason: The algebraic-function rationality result is a known part of Hilbert's 1892 irreducibility work; this is a draft of it, which is of interest but expected. The sketched proof attempt of Noether's claim about quartic surfaces is a mildly notable unpublished detail, but it is incomplete and non-rigorous.

checkable.asserts: The substitution maps t=0 to beta=r/s and t->oo to alpha=p/q.
With z = psi*y, the binomial equation psi*y^n = phi becomes z^n = psi^(n-1)*phi.

checkable.asserts: If f = g2*h2 + l*h3 with l=w, the plane section w=0 factors as two conics.
